answer.evidence: The most clearly trained first-layer units (3, 8, 21, 24, 27, 28) have their largest weights (many 85-99, above the roughly ±80 range seen in near-random units) spread over the central region, about rows 4-19 and cols 4-21, where the nodule sits. Unit 3 (bias -85, all-positive centre) feeds the output positively when propagated through W2 and W3, so a large bright central mass pushes toward malignant. Unit 5 has negative centre weights and pushes toward benign, so a dark or small centre favours benign. Units 18 and 30 also push toward malignant; their centres are negative (unit 18, rows 10-14) or mixed (unit 30), with broadly positive weights in the surround. Several benign-pushing units (2, 14, 16, 19, 25) and malignant-pushing units (18, 30) have scattered positive weights near the image border. Their signs do not line up into one compact region whose sign tracks each unit's effect on the output. I found no corner or edge block where several units share large same-sign weights consistent with their output direction, which is what a pasted marker or artifact usually produces. A few isolated structures (a short vertical run at col 17, rows 3-6 in unit 20; a horizontal run at row 20 in unit 15) are small and not reinforced across units. These look like local anatomical or texture detectors rather than a label shortcut. This conclusion rests on a linear approximation that ignores the ReLUs, so it is uncertain.
answer.main_feature: The model mainly responds to the size and brightness of the central nodule region: several hidden units have broad positive centre weights that push toward malignant, while units favouring a dark or small centre push toward benign. It also uses some texture and brightness of the surrounding peri-nodular tissue.
